To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

humanized mice with reconstituted gastrointestinal tract and human CD4+T cells are susceptible to intrarectally transmitted HIV-1 infection and exhibit systemic infection, CD4+ T-cell depletion and pathology that closely mimics the disease course of HIV infected humans.

intrarectal transmission of HIV-1 to humanized mice results in systemic infection of the mice, depletion of CD4 T cells in the gut-associated lymphoid tissues, and other pathological sequelae that closely mimic those observed in HIV-infected humans.

we developed a novel humanized mouse model that recapitulates the pathogenesis of HIV infection and that this model will allow the development and testing of novel approaches to prevent HIV transmission and to treat HIV infection.

the development of a novel small animal model that recapitulates intrarectal HIV infection and CD4+ depletion in the gastrointestinal tract.
understanding the mechanisms that underlie HIV transmission and the pathogenesis of HIV infection, and developing novel approaches to prevent or treat HIV infection.
the development of a novel model of HIV transmission, infection, and pathogenesis.
